set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
set1.q: Besides signs and symptoms from a structural or functional cardiac problem, what else does clinical heart failure require?
opts: Abnormal pressures measured by right heart catheterization
Catheterization grades hemodynamic severity in selected patients. It is not needed to define clinical heart failure, which uses a natriuretic peptide or evidence of congestion.
Elevated natriuretic peptide or objective cardiogenic congestion
Correct. Clinical heart failure needs the signs and symptoms plus one of two supports: an elevated B-type natriuretic peptide, or objective evidence of cardiogenic pulmonary or systemic congestion.
An ejection fraction measured at 35% or less on imaging
Ejection fraction is not part of the definition; heart failure with a preserved ejection fraction is still heart failure. The added requirement is an elevated natriuretic peptide or congestion.
A documented prior myocardial infarction on the electrocardiogram
Infarction is one cause of heart failure, not a requirement for the diagnosis. The definition asks for an elevated natriuretic peptide or objective congestion.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
set1.q: Which is one of the four basic mechanisms of heart failure?
opts: Reduced blood volume
Volume is increased in the mechanism list, as excessive preload. The four are excess preload, excess afterload, decreased contractility and decreased filling.
Excessive afterload

Correct. The four are increased blood volume (excess preload), increased resistance (excess afterload), decreased contractility and decreased filling. Each leads through acute damage or chronic stress to remodeling.
Increased contractility
Contractility is decreased, not increased, in the mechanism list. The four are excess preload, excess afterload, decreased contractility and decreased filling.
Increased filling
Filling is decreased, not increased. The four mechanisms are excess preload, excess afterload, decreased contractility and decreased filling.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
set1.q: In suspected right-sided heart failure, which test gives the definitive diagnosis?
opts: Natriuretic peptide level
A natriuretic peptide supports a diagnosis of heart failure but cannot say which ventricle has failed. The echocardiogram gives the definitive diagnosis.
Electrocardiogram
The electrocardiogram can show right heart strain but does not diagnose right-sided failure. The echocardiogram gives the definitive diagnosis.
Echocardiogram

Correct. Clinical heart failure with jugular venous distension raises suspicion of right-sided disease, and the echocardiogram gives the definitive diagnosis by ejection fraction. Right heart catheterization then grades hemodynamic severity.
Right heart catheterization
Catheterization measures hemodynamic severity once right-sided failure is suspected or established. The definitive diagnosis comes from the echocardiogram.

set1.io: Compare and contrast precipitating factors, clinical manifestations, diagnosis (including role of B-type natriuretic peptide, BNP), and treatment of acute decompensated heart failure.
set1.q: What is N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide?
opts: An inactive precursor fragment
Correct. It is the inactive precursor fragment released alongside the active hormone. It is more stable, peaks around 24 hours, and is detected earlier and for longer than B-type natriuretic peptide.
The biologically active hormone
The active hormone is B-type natriuretic peptide itself. The N-terminal fragment is an inactive precursor.
The enzyme that degrades the hormone
Neprilysin degrades B-type natriuretic peptide. The N-terminal fragment is an inactive precursor, not an enzyme.
A marker of dead heart muscle
Troponin marks myocardial injury. The N-terminal fragment is an inactive precursor of the natriuretic hormone.

set1.io: Compare and contrast precipitating factors, clinical manifestations, diagnosis (including role of B-type natriuretic peptide, BNP), and treatment of acute decompensated heart failure.
set1.q: What does a clinical diagnosis of congestive heart failure require?
opts: A fourth heart sound heard on auscultation
A fourth heart sound points toward a stiff, hypertrophied ventricle. The requirement for congestive heart failure is congestion, meaning pulmonary or peripheral edema.
Congestion, meaning pulmonary or peripheral edema

Correct. Clinical heart failure means the patient is symptomatic, and calling it congestive requires congestion, which is edema in the lungs, the periphery or both. Fatigue and exertional dyspnea without edema do not meet it.
An ejection fraction within the reduced range
Congestion, not the ejection fraction group, is what makes heart failure congestive. A patient with a preserved ejection fraction and edema qualifies.
Symptoms lasting longer than one full year
More than a year of symptoms defines chronic heart failure. Congestive describes the presence of edema, which is a separate question from duration.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
set1.q: Which drug class is recommended to prevent heart failure in patients with diabetes who have no structural heart disease?
opts: Beta blocker started at diagnosis
A beta blocker is not part of stage A prevention; it is a stage B therapy once structural disease appears. Prevention in diabetes uses a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
Angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor
This combination belongs to symptomatic reduced ejection fraction in functional class II or III. Stage A prevention in diabetes uses a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
Hydralazine with isosorbide dinitrate
This pairing is reserved for African American patients with reduced ejection fraction in functional class III or IV. Stage A prevention uses a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor

Correct. Prevention in stage A, risk factors with a normal heart, carries one strong drug recommendation: a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor for patients with diabetes, ahead of any beta blocker, which is a stage B therapy.

set1.io: Differentiate between systolic dysfunction and diastolic dysfunction..
set1.q: In the diastolic heart failure chain, how does edema progress?
opts: Peripheral only, never pulmonary
The diastolic chain does reach the lungs. It gives peripheral edema first and then pulmonary edema.
Peripheral first, then pulmonary
Correct. The diastolic chain ends in peripheral edema and then pulmonary edema, while the systolic chain goes straight to pulmonary edema. The order is one of the discriminators between them.
Pulmonary first, then peripheral
That reverses the diastolic order. The systolic chain ends in pulmonary edema; the diastolic chain gives peripheral edema first, then pulmonary.
Pulmonary only, never peripheral
That is closer to the systolic chain. Diastolic failure gives peripheral edema first and then pulmonary edema.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
set1.q: Which referral accompanies optimized therapy after acute heart failure leaves the ejection fraction below 35%?
opts: Cardiac rehabilitation

Correct. Cardiac rehabilitation runs alongside optimized guideline-directed therapy while the patient wears a defibrillator vest, before the echocardiogram is repeated to decide on an implantable device.
Hospice enrollment
Hospice is not part of this recovery pathway. Cardiac rehabilitation accompanies optimized therapy before the echocardiogram is repeated.
Transplant evaluation
Transplant is reserved for failure that progresses despite management. After an acute event the referral is to cardiac rehabilitation.
Valve surgery review
Valve surgery is not part of this pathway. Cardiac rehabilitation accompanies optimized therapy before the echocardiogram is repeated.

set1.io: Define the following diagnostic and therapeutic groups of HF patients, and the treatment implications/recommendations for each group: a. HF with reduced EF (HFrEF) b. HF with mildly reduced EF (HFmrEF) c. HF with preserved EF (HFpEF)
set1.q: Which ejection fraction range defines heart failure with mildly reduced ejection fraction?
opts: That range is preserved ejection fraction, 50% or more. Mildly reduced is 41 to 49%.
That range is well within reduced ejection fraction and overlaps the device threshold. Mildly reduced is 41 to 49%.
Correct. Mildly reduced ejection fraction is 41 to 49%. It sits between reduced at 40% or less and preserved at 50% or more, and its treatment resembles that of preserved ejection fraction.
That range falls within reduced ejection fraction, 40% or less. Mildly reduced is 41 to 49%.

set1.io: Compare and contrast precipitating factors, clinical manifestations, diagnosis (including role of B-type natriuretic peptide, BNP), and treatment of acute decompensated heart failure.
set1.q: Which bedside hemodynamic profile describes congestion with adequate perfusion?
opts: Warm and wet
Correct. The four profiles cross congestion with perfusion: warm and dry is normal, warm and wet is congestion, cold and dry is hypoperfusion, and cold and wet is hypoperfusion with congestion.
Warm and dry
Warm and dry is the normal profile, with neither congestion nor low perfusion. Congestion with adequate perfusion is warm and wet.
Cold and dry
Cold and dry is hypoperfusion without congestion. Congestion with adequate perfusion is warm and wet.
Cold and wet
Cold and wet combines hypoperfusion with congestion. Congestion with adequate perfusion is warm and wet.

set1.io: Define the following diagnostic and therapeutic groups of HF patients, and the treatment implications/recommendations for each group: a. HF with reduced EF (HFrEF) b. HF with mildly reduced EF (HFmrEF) c. HF with preserved EF (HFpEF)
set1.q: Which therapy carries the strongest recommendation in mildly reduced ejection fraction?
opts: Neprilysin inhibitor combination
The angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor is a weak recommendation in mildly reduced ejection fraction. Diuretics as needed carry the strongest one.
Diuretics as needed

Correct. In mildly reduced ejection fraction diuretics as needed are the one strong recommendation; the sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor is moderate, and renin-angiotensin blockade, the antagonist and the beta blocker are weak.
Evidence-based beta blocker
The beta blocker is a weak recommendation in mildly reduced ejection fraction. Diuretics as needed carry the strongest one.
Mineralocorticoid antagonist
The mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist is a weak recommendation here. Diuretics as needed carry the strongest recommendation.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
set1.q: Which description defines heart failure?
opts: Persistently low systolic blood pressure from any cause
Low pressure has many causes outside the heart. Heart failure is defined by inadequate cardiac output for metabolic demand or output achieved only at high filling pressures.
Blockage of coronary flow causing death of heart muscle
That describes myocardial infarction, which is one cause of ischemic cardiomyopathy. Heart failure is the pumping syndrome that can follow it, not the infarct itself.
Output below demand, or met only at high filling pressures

Correct. The heart cannot pump blood at a rate that meets the body's metabolic needs at rest and during effort, or manages it only because filling pressures are abnormally high. That second half is why a normal output does not exclude the syndrome.
Any ejection fraction that falls below the normal range
Ejection fraction sorts heart failure into groups, but a preserved ejection fraction does not exclude it. The definition rests on inadequate output or high filling pressures.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
set1.q: Which blood test anchors the laboratory workup of suspected heart failure?
opts: B-type natriuretic peptide

Correct. The natriuretic peptide is the key laboratory test: it supports the clinical diagnosis, rules acute heart failure out below 100, and carries prognostic weight. The blood count, metabolic panel and troponin play supporting roles.
Cardiac troponin level
Troponin is ordered selectively, when an infarction or ischemic cardiomyopathy is suspected. The anchoring test is the B-type natriuretic peptide.
Complete blood count
The blood count helps with the differential diagnosis, for example anemia. The anchoring test for heart failure is the B-type natriuretic peptide.
Serum potassium alone
Potassium is followed on the metabolic panel for therapy safety. The anchoring test for suspected heart failure is the B-type natriuretic peptide.

set1.io: Differentiate between systolic dysfunction and diastolic dysfunction..
set1.q: Diastolic heart failure traces back to which cardiomyopathy?
opts: Dilated cardiomyopathy
Dilated, thin, ballooned muscle contracts poorly, which is the systolic chain rather than the diastolic one. Diastolic failure traces to hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
Ischemic cardiomyopathy
Ischemic cardiomyopathy leads the systolic chain along with dilated cardiomyopathy. Diastolic failure traces to hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
Toxin-related cardiomyopathy
Toxins such as alcohol and chemotherapy cause heart failure, but the diastolic chain is anchored to hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

Correct. Increased muscle contracts strongly but relaxes poorly, so filling suffers. The chain runs diastolic failure, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, hypertension, a fourth heart sound, then peripheral and pulmonary edema.

set1.io: Define the following diagnostic and therapeutic groups of HF patients, and the treatment implications/recommendations for each group: a. HF with reduced EF (HFrEF) b. HF with mildly reduced EF (HFmrEF) c. HF with preserved EF (HFpEF)
set1.q: An ejection fraction that rises from 30% to 46% on treatment is classified as which group?
opts: Mildly reduced ejection fraction
46% alone would be mildly reduced, but the history of 30% changes the label. A reduced value that recovers above 40% is improved ejection fraction.
Preserved ejection fraction
Preserved ejection fraction is 50% or more, which 46% has not reached. The recovery from 30% makes this improved ejection fraction.
Reduced ejection fraction
The value is no longer in the reduced range of 40% or less. Recovery from 30% to above 40% is improved ejection fraction.
Improved ejection fraction
Correct. A previous value in the reduced range that has recovered above 40% is improved ejection fraction, even though the new number alone would fall in the mildly reduced band.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
set1.q: Which toxins cause heart failure?
opts: Caffeine and nicotine gum
These are not among the toxic causes. The toxins that cause heart failure are alcohol and chemotherapy.
Lead and arsenic salts
Lead and arsenic are not among the toxic causes of heart failure. Alcohol and chemotherapy are the toxic causes of heart failure.
Aspirin and acetaminophen
Common analgesics such as these are not toxic causes of heart failure. Alcohol and chemotherapy are the toxic causes of heart failure.
Alcohol and chemotherapy
Correct. Toxins such as alcohol and chemotherapy sit among the non-ischemic causes of heart failure, alongside hypertension, valvular disease and autoimmune or metabolic disease.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
set1.q: Which workup is used for suspected high-output heart failure?
opts: Troponin and a stress test only
Those look for ischemia. The high-output workup is echocardiogram, complete blood count, complete metabolic panel and natriuretic peptide.
Chest radiograph and spirometry
Those look toward the lungs. The high-output workup is echocardiogram, complete blood count, complete metabolic panel and natriuretic peptide.
Echo, blood count, metabolic panel, peptide
Correct. The high-output workup is an echocardiogram, complete blood count, complete metabolic panel and B-type natriuretic peptide. The blood count matters because anemia is one of its causes.
Right heart catheterization by itself
Catheterization grades hemodynamic severity in right-sided failure and is not the high-output workup, which is echocardiogram, blood count, metabolic panel and natriuretic peptide.

set1.io: Identify medical care strategies for heart failure in the lecture topic list for the following populations. 1. infant 2. child 3. adolescent 4. adult 5. elderly
set1.q: Among patients older than 65 with heart failure, what is the one-year mortality after a hospitalization?
opts: About 35%
Correct. One-year mortality after a heart failure hospitalization is about 35% in this older group, which is why heart failure is described as a syndrome with reduced longevity.
About 5%
That badly understates the risk. About 35% of these patients die within a year of a heart failure hospitalization.
About 15%
That still understates it. One-year mortality after a heart failure hospitalization is about 35% in patients older than 65.
About 70%
That overstates it. One-year mortality after a heart failure hospitalization is about 35% in patients older than 65.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
set1.q: Which drugs are sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors used in heart failure?
opts: Dapagliflozin and empagliflozin
Correct. Dapagliflozin and empagliflozin are the sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors, recommended from stage A in diabetes through every symptomatic ejection fraction group.
Spironolactone and eplerenone
These are mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, the potassium-sparing diuretics. The sodium-glucose inhibitors are dapagliflozin and empagliflozin.
Losartan and irbesartan
These are angiotensin II receptor blockers. The sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors are dapagliflozin and empagliflozin.
Furosemide and bumetanide
These are loop diuretics, which waste potassium. The sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors are dapagliflozin and empagliflozin.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
set1.q: What should a patient starting a loop diuretic expect to have monitored?
opts: Natriuretic peptide weekly
The natriuretic peptide is a diagnostic and prognostic marker, not diuretic safety monitoring. Potassium and renal function are what are followed.
Potassium and kidney function
Correct. Loop diuretics waste potassium, so potassium and renal function are followed on the metabolic panel. The same monitoring applies in the other direction for the potassium-sparing antagonists.
Liver enzymes and bilirubin
Liver tests are not the monitoring that a loop diuretic calls for. Potassium and renal function are followed on the metabolic panel.
Thyroid-stimulating hormone
Thyroid function is not the monitoring a loop diuretic needs. Potassium and renal function are followed on the metabolic panel.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
set1.q: What guidance applies to verapamil and diltiazem in heart failure?
opts: Prefer them to beta blockers
Beta blockers are core heart failure therapy, while calcium channel blockers such as verapamil and diltiazem are avoided.
Give them in any class
Calcium channel blockers such as verapamil and diltiazem are avoided in heart failure regardless of symptom class.
Avoid them
Correct. Verapamil and diltiazem are calcium channel blockers, and calcium channel blockers are avoided in heart failure. Rate and pressure control come from the recommended classes instead.
Use them first-line
They are not first-line in heart failure; calcium channel blockers are avoided. First-line therapy depends on stage and ejection fraction group.

set1.io: Define the following diagnostic and therapeutic groups of HF patients, and the treatment implications/recommendations for each group: a. HF with reduced EF (HFrEF) b. HF with mildly reduced EF (HFmrEF) c. HF with preserved EF (HFpEF)
set1.q: Which patients with reduced ejection fraction receive hydralazine with isosorbide dinitrate?
opts: African American patients in functional class III or IV

Correct. Hydralazine with nitrates carries a strong recommendation in reduced ejection fraction for African American patients in New York Heart Association class III or IV, added to the core drug classes.
Every patient in functional class I or II at diagnosis
The pairing is not for mild, early disease. It is recommended for African American patients with reduced ejection fraction in functional class III or IV.
Patients with preserved ejection fraction
It does not appear in the preserved ejection fraction recommendations. It is for African American patients with reduced ejection fraction in functional class III or IV.
At-risk patients who also have diabetes

At-risk patients with diabetes receive a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor. Hydralazine with nitrates is for African American patients with reduced ejection fraction in functional class III or IV.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
set1.q: Which renal complication of heart failure reflects inadequate perfusion?
opts: Nephrotic syndrome with heavy proteinuria
Nephrotic syndrome is a primary kidney disorder, not the renal complication described. Heart failure causes acute kidney injury with decreased urine output.
Kidney stones from urinary stasis
Stones are not the renal complication of heart failure. Poor perfusion causes acute kidney injury with decreased urine output.
Polyuria from excess filtration
Output falls rather than rises. Heart failure causes acute kidney injury with decreased urine output.
Acute kidney injury with low urine output
Correct. Renal dysfunction in heart failure presents as acute kidney injury with decreased urine output, one of the signs of inadequate tissue perfusion.

set1.io: Identify medical care strategies for heart failure in the lecture topic list for the following populations. 1. infant 2. child 3. adolescent 4. adult 5. elderly
set1.q: Which N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide level suggests heart failure in a patient younger than 75?
opts: Above 900
900 is a B-type natriuretic peptide threshold for acute failure. For the N-terminal fragment under 75, heart failure is likely above 125.
Above 2,000
That sets the bar far too high. Younger than 75, an N-terminal fragment above 125 makes heart failure likely.
Above 125
Correct. Younger than 75, a level above 125 makes heart failure likely; older than 75 the threshold rises to 450. Age changes how the same number is read.
Above 450
450 is the threshold for patients older than 75. Younger than 75, heart failure is likely above 125.

set1.io: Define each class of the New York Heart Association (NYHA) symptomatic and functional classification of heart failure.
set1.q: What separates New York Heart Association class II from class III?
opts: Class III needs only slight exertion
Correct. Both are free of symptoms at rest. Class II has symptoms with exertion, while class III has them with slight exertion, so the amount of effort that provokes symptoms separates them.
Class III has symptoms at rest
Symptoms at rest define class IV, not class III. Class III differs from class II by needing only slight exertion.
Class II has no symptoms at all
No symptoms is class I. Class II has symptoms with exertion; class III with only slight exertion.
Class III requires structural disease
The classes grade symptoms, not structure. Class III differs from class II by symptoms with only slight exertion.

set1.io: Compare and contrast precipitating factors, clinical manifestations, diagnosis (including role of B-type natriuretic peptide, BNP), and treatment of acute decompensated heart failure.
set1.q: Which predischarge B-type natriuretic peptide is linked to a lower risk of 30-day readmission?
opts: Below 1,500
That bar is too generous. The level linked to lower 30-day readmission is below 430.
Below 430
Correct. A predischarge level below 430 carries a lower risk of readmission within 30 days, which makes the level a guide to readiness for discharge.
Above 430
A higher level marks greater risk, not less. A predischarge level below 430 is linked to lower 30-day readmission.
Above 900
Above 900 acute heart failure is likely, the opposite of readiness. A predischarge level below 430 is linked to lower readmission.

set1.io: Differentiate each stage of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA), natural history classification of heart failure, and associated treatment recommendations of each stage.
set1.q: Structural heart disease with symptoms that have since resolved on treatment belongs to which stage?
opts: Stage D
Stage D is advanced heart failure. Structural disease whose symptoms have resolved on therapy is stage C.
Stage C
Correct. Stage C is symptomatic structural heart disease, past or current. Once symptoms have occurred the patient stays in stage C when they resolve; the stages do not move backward.
Stage B
Stage B is structural disease that has never caused symptoms. Past symptoms keep a patient in stage C even after they resolve.
Stage A
Stage A is risk factors with a normal heart. A patient with structural disease and past symptoms is stage C.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
set1.q: Which metabolic condition is a risk factor for heart failure?
opts: Iron overload from diet alone
Dietary iron is not on the list. Obesity and metabolic syndrome are risk factors, along with diabetes and hypertension.
Low blood cholesterol levels
Low cholesterol is not a risk factor. Obesity and metabolic syndrome are, along with diabetes, hypertension and coronary artery disease.
Obesity or metabolic syndrome
Correct. Obesity and metabolic syndrome are risk factors, along with diabetes, hypertension and coronary artery disease. They are also targets a patient can change.
Low body mass with good fitness
Leanness and fitness are not risk factors. Obesity and metabolic syndrome are, along with diabetes and hypertension.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
set1.q: Which murmur accompanies mitral stenosis as a cause of right-sided heart failure?
opts: Holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border
That describes tricuspid regurgitation, which accompanies pulmonary arterial hypertension. Mitral stenosis gives a rumbling diastolic murmur at the apex with an opening snap.
Systolic murmur at the base radiating to the neck
A basal systolic murmur radiating to the neck is the pattern of aortic stenosis, a left-sided lesion. Mitral stenosis gives a rumbling diastolic murmur at the apex with an opening snap.
Continuous murmur beneath the left clavicle
A continuous murmur does not belong to any of the three causes of right-sided failure. Mitral stenosis gives a rumbling diastolic murmur at the apex with an opening snap.
Diastolic rumble at the apex with an opening snap

Correct. Mitral stenosis gives a rumbling diastolic murmur at the apex with an opening snap. It is one of the three causes of right-sided failure, alongside chronic left-sided failure and pulmonary arterial hypertension.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
set1.q: What are the goals of treatment in chronic heart failure?
opts: Cure of the cardiomyopathy in every case
Cure is not among the goals. Treatment aims to decrease symptoms, increase survival and limit disease progression.
A normal ejection fraction in every patient
A normal ejection fraction is not the target. Treatment aims to decrease symptoms, increase survival and limit disease progression.
Stopping all drugs once symptoms settle
Symptom relief is one goal, but survival and slowing progression are the others, so therapy continues. The goals are fewer symptoms, longer survival and slower progression.
Fewer symptoms, longer life, slower disease
Correct. The three goals are to decrease symptoms, increase survival and limit disease progression. That is why several drug classes are combined even when a patient feels well.

set2.io: Compare and contrast precipitating factors, clinical manifestations, diagnosis (including role of B-type natriuretic peptide, BNP), and treatment of acute decompensated heart failure.
set2.q: After acute heart failure from infarction leaves the ejection fraction below 35%, what comes first for sudden death protection?
opts: Home inotropes until the heart recovers
Inotropes are for intensive care use only. The first step is a wearable defibrillator while guideline-directed therapy is optimized.
A wearable defibrillator while therapy is optimized

Correct. The pathway is a wearable defibrillator vest, then optimized guideline-directed therapy and cardiac rehabilitation, then a repeat echocardiogram, and an implantable defibrillator only if the ejection fraction has not improved.
An implantable defibrillator before discharge
An implantable device comes last, only if a repeat echocardiogram shows no improvement after therapy has been optimized. A wearable defibrillator comes first.
Heart transplant listing at the first admission
Transplant is an end-stage option, not the first response to a new low ejection fraction. The first step is a wearable defibrillator while therapy is optimized.

set2.io: Define the following diagnostic and therapeutic groups of HF patients, and the treatment implications/recommendations for each group: a. HF with reduced EF (HFrEF) b. HF with mildly reduced EF (HFmrEF) c. HF with preserved EF (HFpEF)
set2.q: After diuretics, which drug class has the next strongest recommendation in preserved ejection fraction?
opts: Hydralazine with a nitrate
Hydralazine with nitrates is a reduced ejection fraction therapy for selected patients. In preserved ejection fraction the next strongest after diuretics is the sodium-glucose inhibitor.
Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor

Correct. In preserved ejection fraction, diuretics as needed are strong and the sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor is moderate. The neprilysin combination, the mineralocorticoid antagonist and the receptor blocker are weak.
Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist
The mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist is only a weak recommendation in preserved ejection fraction. The next strongest after diuretics is the sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
Angiotensin II receptor blocker
The angiotensin receptor blocker is a weak recommendation here. After diuretics, the sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor carries the next strongest.

set2.io: Define the following diagnostic and therapeutic groups of HF patients, and the treatment implications/recommendations for each group: a. HF with reduced EF (HFrEF) b. HF with mildly reduced EF (HFmrEF) c. HF with preserved EF (HFpEF)
set2.q: Which ejection fraction range defines heart failure with reduced ejection fraction?
opts: That range defines heart failure with mildly reduced ejection fraction. The reduced group is 40% or less.
50% or more
That is the preserved range, which is also the normal ejection fraction. Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction is 40% or less.
That range sits within normal and preserved ejection fraction. Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction is 40% or less.
40% or less
Correct. Reduced ejection fraction is 40% or less, mildly reduced is 41 to 49%, and preserved is 50% or more. The reduced group carries the fullest set of strongly recommended drug classes.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
set2.q: Which of these is a risk factor for heart failure?
opts: Regular aerobic exercise
Exercise is not a risk factor. The list includes chronic tachyarrhythmias, hypertension, diabetes, obesity and tobacco, among others.
Low dietary potassium
Low dietary potassium is not a heart failure risk factor. Chronic tachyarrhythmias are, along with hypertension, diabetes and coronary artery disease.
Chronic bradycardia
Chronic slow rhythms are not a heart failure risk factor; fast ones are. Chronic tachyarrhythmias are, along with hypertension, diabetes and coronary artery disease.
Chronic tachyarrhythmias
Correct. Chronic tachyarrhythmias sit on the risk factor list with age, hypertension, coronary artery disease, diabetes, obesity, alcohol, tobacco, family history, genetics and cardiotoxic medicines.

set2.io: Differentiate each stage of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA), natural history classification of heart failure, and associated treatment recommendations of each stage.
set2.q: For a patient at risk for heart failure who has diabetes, which drug class is recommended first?
opts: Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor

Correct. In stage A, at risk for heart failure, the one strongly recommended drug is a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor in patients with diabetes. A beta blocker enters only at stage B, once structural disease exists.
Beta blocker as the first agent
A beta blocker is not recommended in stage A. It enters at stage B. The first drug for an at-risk patient with diabetes is a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist
These belong to symptomatic heart failure, strongly for reduced ejection fraction. In stage A with diabetes the drug is a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
Loop diuretic such as furosemide
Diuretics treat congestion, which a stage A patient does not have. The recommended drug for an at-risk patient with diabetes is a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.

set2.io: Compare and contrast precipitating factors, clinical manifestations, diagnosis (including role of B-type natriuretic peptide, BNP), and treatment of acute decompensated heart failure.
set2.q: A patient with long-standing heart failure develops a sudden worsening. How is the episode classified?
opts: Acute on chronic heart failure

Correct. In the sequence pre-heart failure, acute new onset, resolution, exacerbation, chronic heart failure and acute on chronic heart failure, a sudden worsening on a background of chronic disease is acute on chronic heart failure.
Acute new-onset heart failure
New-onset heart failure is the first symptomatic episode in someone without prior heart failure. A sudden worsening of established chronic disease is acute on chronic heart failure.
Pre-heart failure with new symptoms
Pre-heart failure is by definition asymptomatic structural disease. A symptomatic worsening of known chronic disease is acute on chronic heart failure.
High-output heart failure
High-output failure describes elevated cardiac output from increased peripheral demand such as anemia. It says nothing about a sudden worsening of chronic disease.

set2.io: Differentiate each stage of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA), natural history classification of heart failure, and associated treatment recommendations of each stage.
set2.q: Which drug class carries a strong recommendation in stage B but not in stage A?
opts: Hydralazine-nitrate
That pairing belongs to stage C and D reduced ejection fraction in African American patients in functional class III or IV. Stage B adds a beta blocker.
Beta blocker

Correct. Stage B, pre-heart failure, adds an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor and a beta blocker, with an angiotensin receptor blocker if the inhibitor is not tolerated. Stage A carries only the sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor for diabetes.
Sodium-glucose inhibitor
The sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor for diabetes appears in both stage A and stage B. The class that stage B adds is the beta blocker, with angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibition.
Loop diuretic
Diuretics are given as needed for congestion in symptomatic stages C and D. Stage B adds a beta blocker and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibition.

set2.io: Define each class of the New York Heart Association (NYHA) symptomatic and functional classification of heart failure.
set2.q: What defines New York Heart Association class I?
opts: No symptoms
Correct. Class I is no symptoms, class II is symptoms with exertion, class III is symptoms with slight exertion, and class IV is symptoms at rest. The classes grade symptoms, not structure.
Symptoms with exertion
Symptoms brought on by ordinary exertion define class II. Class I is the absence of any heart failure symptoms.
Symptoms with slight exertion
Symptoms with only slight exertion define class III. Class I is the absence of any heart failure symptoms.
Symptoms at rest
Symptoms at rest define class IV, the most severe class. Class I is no symptoms.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
set2.q: What proportion of heart failure is left-sided?
opts: About half
That understates it. Left-sided heart failure makes up 70 to 80% of cases, far more than right-sided or combined failure.
Nearly 100%
That overstates it. Right-sided and combined failure exist in their own right; left-sided failure is 70 to 80% of cases.
Correct. Left-sided heart failure is by far the most common, at 70 to 80% of cases, and it is also the most common cause of right-sided heart failure.
That reverses the balance. Left-sided failure accounts for 70 to 80% of heart failure, far more than right-sided disease.

set2.io: Differentiate each stage of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA), natural history classification of heart failure, and associated treatment recommendations of each stage.
set2.q: Which heart failure stage is also called pre-heart failure?
opts: Stage A
Stage A is at risk for heart failure, with a normal heart. Pre-heart failure is stage B.
Stage C
Stage C is symptomatic heart failure. Pre-heart failure is stage B, where structural disease has not yet caused symptoms.
Stage D
Stage D is advanced heart failure. Pre-heart failure is stage B, structural disease without symptoms.
Stage B

Correct. Stage B, pre-heart failure, is structural heart disease without symptoms, such as ischemic cardiomyopathy or left ventricular hypertrophy. Its therapy adds renin-angiotensin blockade and a beta blocker.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
set2.q: What defines high-output heart failure?
opts: Normal output with high filling pressures
Normal output at high filling pressure is part of the general definition. High-output failure is elevated output from faster rate and contraction.
Low output from a stiff, thick ventricle
A stiff hypertrophied ventricle is the diastolic chain. High-output failure is elevated output from faster rate and contraction.
Elevated output from faster rate and contraction

Correct. High-output failure is elevated cardiac output from increased heart rate and contractility, meeting an increased peripheral demand; over time it may lead to ischemic cardiomyopathy or remodeling.
Low output from weak ventricular contraction
Weak contraction with low output is the systolic chain. High-output failure is elevated output driven by demand.

set2.io: Compare and contrast precipitating factors, clinical manifestations, diagnosis (including role of B-type natriuretic peptide, BNP), and treatment of acute decompensated heart failure.
set2.q: Which natriuretic peptide result is altered by an angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor?
opts: B-type natriuretic peptide

Correct. Neprilysin degrades B-type natriuretic peptide, so blocking it with sacubitril-valsartan alters that result. Knowing whether the test was the peptide or its N-terminal fragment matters in these patients.
N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide
The N-terminal fragment is not the one tied to neprilysin. B-type natriuretic peptide is degraded by neprilysin and so is altered by the drug.
Both peptides to the same degree
Only B-type natriuretic peptide is linked to neprilysin degradation. That is why it is the result an angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor alters.
Neither peptide in any meaningful way
The effect is real: neprilysin degrades B-type natriuretic peptide, so blocking neprilysin alters that result.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
set2.q: How is congestive heart failure diagnosed?
opts: By a natriuretic peptide level interpreted on its own
A natriuretic peptide supports the diagnosis only alongside signs and symptoms of heart failure. On its own it does not make a clinical diagnosis.
Clinically, from signs and symptoms plus supporting evidence

Correct. Congestive heart failure is a clinical diagnosis: signs and symptoms of heart failure plus an elevated B-type natriuretic peptide or cardiogenic pulmonary or systemic congestion. No single test makes the diagnosis alone.
By an ejection fraction measurement on echocardiography alone

Echocardiography classifies heart failure by ejection fraction and shows structure, but a number alone is not the diagnosis. The diagnosis is clinical, built on signs, symptoms and supporting evidence.
By right heart catheterization performed in every patient
Right heart catheterization is reserved for grading hemodynamic severity. The diagnosis of congestive heart failure is made clinically.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
set2.q: Which heart failure risk factors can a patient change?
opts: Age, genetics and prior infarction
Age and genetics cannot be changed, and a past infarction cannot be undone. Tobacco, excess alcohol and obesity are the modifiable targets.
Family history and advancing age
Neither can be changed. Tobacco, excess alcohol and obesity are the risk factors a patient can modify.
Tobacco, excess alcohol and obesity
Correct. These are modifiable, so they are the targets of prevention counseling. Age, family history and genetic abnormality are risk factors a patient cannot change.
Age, family history and genetics
These are real risk factors, but none can be changed. Tobacco, excess alcohol and obesity are the modifiable ones.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
set2.q: Why is a complete metabolic panel ordered in heart failure?
opts: To exclude myocardial infarction
Troponin is the test when infarction or ischemic cardiomyopathy is a concern. The metabolic panel follows potassium and renal function.
To follow potassium and renal function

Correct. The panel tracks electrolytes, potassium above all, and renal function through blood urea nitrogen, creatinine and filtration rate. Both matter because diuretics and several therapies move potassium and affect the kidneys.
To measure the natriuretic peptide
The natriuretic peptide is a separate test. The metabolic panel is ordered for potassium and renal function.
To detect anemia as a contributor
Anemia is found on the complete blood count, which helps the differential diagnosis. The metabolic panel follows potassium and renal function.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
set2.q: What is the lifetime risk of developing heart failure?
opts: About one in four
Correct. Lifetime risk is 24%, about one in four, and about 6.7 million Americans older than 20 have heart failure. The burden rises steeply with age.
About one in twenty
One in twenty badly understates it. The lifetime risk of heart failure is about 24%, roughly one person in four.
About one in ten
One in ten still understates it. The lifetime risk of heart failure is about 24%, roughly one person in four.
About one in two
One in two overstates it. The lifetime risk of heart failure is about 24%, roughly one person in four.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
set2.q: Which findings reflect portal overload in right-sided heart failure?
opts: Peripheral edema and distended neck veins
These are right-sided findings too, but they reflect systemic overload. Portal overload shows as nausea, loss of appetite and hepatomegaly.
Orthopnea, crackles and a third heart sound
These point to the left side: pulmonary congestion and rapid filling of a dilated left ventricle. Portal overload shows as nausea, poor appetite and hepatomegaly.
Narrow pulse pressure and cool extremities
These are signs of low perfusion rather than congestion. Portal overload in right-sided failure shows as nausea, poor appetite and hepatomegaly.
Nausea, poor appetite and hepatomegaly

Correct. Right ventricular failure backs fluid up. Portal overload gives nausea, loss of appetite and hepatomegaly with congestion or ascites, while systemic overload gives peripheral edema and jugular venous distension.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
set2.q: What does cardiac remodeling consist of?
opts: Myocyte regeneration and scar resorption
Remodeling is not repair. It consists of myocyte hypertrophy and collagen fibrosis driven by damage and neurohormonal activation.
Valve calcification and annular widening
Those are valve changes rather than remodeling of the myocardium, which consists of myocyte hypertrophy and collagen fibrosis.
Coronary plaque rupture and thrombosis
Plaque rupture causes infarction, one route to damage. Remodeling itself is myocyte hypertrophy and collagen fibrosis.
Myocyte hypertrophy and collagen fibrosis
Correct. Acute damage or chronic conditions drive remodeling, which is myocyte hypertrophy and collagen fibrosis. Neurohormonal activation, inflammation and mechanical stress push it along.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
set2.q: Which drug is the angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor?
opts: Hydralazine-dinitrate
Hydralazine with isosorbide dinitrate is a separate pairing for selected African American patients. The angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor is sacubitril-valsartan.
Sacubitril-valsartan

Correct. Sacubitril-valsartan pairs an angiotensin II receptor blocker with a neprilysin inhibitor. It is recommended in reduced ejection fraction for class II or III, and it alters the B-type natriuretic peptide result.
Lisinopril alone
Lisinopril is an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor, not a neprilysin combination. The angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor is sacubitril-valsartan.
Valsartan alone
Valsartan alone is an angiotensin II receptor blocker without the neprilysin component. The combination is sacubitril-valsartan.

set2.io: Define the following diagnostic and therapeutic groups of HF patients, and the treatment implications/recommendations for each group: a. HF with reduced EF (HFrEF) b. HF with mildly reduced EF (HFmrEF) c. HF with preserved EF (HFpEF)
set2.q: Which combination reflects core therapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction?
opts: Inotrope, nitrate, diuretic and calcium blocker

Inotropes are intensive-care-only and calcium channel blockers are avoided. The reduced ejection fraction core is a beta blocker, renin-angiotensin blockade, the mineralocorticoid antagonist and the sodium-glucose inhibitor.
Beta blocker, lisinopril, spironolactone, dapagliflozin

Correct. The core is a beta blocker, a renin-angiotensin blocker such as lisinopril (or an angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor, converting enzyme inhibitor or receptor blocker), a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist such as spironolactone and a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor such as dapagliflozin, with diuretics as needed.
Calcium blocker, beta blocker, diuretic and inotrope

Calcium channel blockers are avoided in heart failure and inotropes are for the intensive care unit. The core is a beta blocker, renin-angiotensin blockade, the mineralocorticoid antagonist and the sodium-glucose inhibitor.
Diuretic alone, adding others only for comorbidities
That describes preserved and mildly reduced ejection fraction, where diuretics lead and other classes serve comorbidities. Reduced ejection fraction uses all four core classes.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
set2.q: What is the most common valvular cause of heart failure?
opts: Tricuspid regurgitation
Tricuspid regurgitation is a murmur heard with pulmonary arterial hypertension in right-sided failure. The most common valvular cause is aortic stenosis.
Pulmonic stenosis
Pulmonic stenosis is not the leading valvular cause. The most common valvular cause of heart failure is aortic stenosis.
Aortic stenosis
Correct. Valvular disease is among the causes of heart failure, and aortic stenosis is the most common valvular one. Mitral stenosis appears instead as a cause of right-sided failure.
Mitral stenosis
Mitral stenosis is a cause of right-sided heart failure. The most common valvular cause of heart failure overall is aortic stenosis.

set2.io: Identify medical care strategies for heart failure in the lecture topic list for the following populations. 1. infant 2. child 3. adolescent 4. adult 5. elderly
set2.q: Which N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide level suggests heart failure in a patient older than 75?
opts: Above 3,000
That sets the bar far too high. Older than 75, an N-terminal fragment above 450 makes heart failure likely.
Above 450
Correct. Older than 75, heart failure is likely above 450, compared with above 125 in younger patients. The higher threshold is the one age-specific rule for elderly patients.
Above 125
125 is the threshold for patients younger than 75. Older than 75, heart failure is likely above 450.
Above 100
100 is the B-type natriuretic peptide rule-out level. For the N-terminal fragment over 75, heart failure is likely above 450.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
set2.q: How is high-output heart failure treated?
opts: Treat the underlying cause and add a diuretic
Correct. High-output failure is driven by peripheral demand, so treatment targets the cause, such as anemia, hyperthyroidism or an arteriovenous fistula, with a diuretic for congestion.
Inotropes in the intensive care unit
Inotropes raise output further and are intensive-care-only. High-output failure is treated by correcting the cause, with a diuretic.
A calcium channel blocker to slow the rate
Calcium channel blockers are avoided in heart failure. High-output failure is treated by correcting the cause, with a diuretic.
Early referral for heart transplant
Transplant does not address a problem of excess peripheral demand. High-output failure is treated by correcting the cause, with a diuretic.

set2.io: Differentiate each stage of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA), natural history classification of heart failure, and associated treatment recommendations of each stage.
set2.q: Why is a beta blocker the wrong first choice for an at-risk patient with diabetes and a normal heart?
opts: Diabetes makes any drug unnecessary
Diabetes is exactly what triggers treatment in stage A: a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
A loop diuretic must be started first
A stage A patient has no congestion to treat. The first drug is a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
The first drug is a sodium-glucose inhibitor
Correct. In stage A the only strongly recommended drug is a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor in patients with diabetes. The beta blocker is a stage B therapy once structural disease exists.
Beta blockers are banned in all heart failure
Beta blockers are core therapy in reduced ejection fraction and a stage B recommendation. They are simply not the first choice in stage A.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
set2.q: How does the murmur of tricuspid regurgitation change with breathing?
opts: Louder on expiration
The change runs the other way. The holosystolic murmur of tricuspid regurgitation grows louder on inspiration.
Silent on inspiration
It does not disappear. The tricuspid regurgitation murmur is holosystolic and grows louder on inspiration.
Unchanged by breathing
It does vary with respiration. The holosystolic murmur of tricuspid regurgitation grows louder on inspiration.
Louder on inspiration
Correct. Tricuspid regurgitation, which accompanies pulmonary arterial hypertension in right-sided failure, is a holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that grows louder on inspiration.

set2.io: Compare and contrast precipitating factors, clinical manifestations, diagnosis (including role of B-type natriuretic peptide, BNP), and treatment of acute decompensated heart failure.
set2.q: What does a B-type natriuretic peptide level below 100 indicate?
opts: Acute heart failure is ruled out

Correct. A level below 100 rules out acute heart failure with a negative predictive value above 90%. From 100 to 400 the test has no useful sensitivity or specificity, above 400 heart failure is likely, and above 900 acute heart failure is likely.
Heart failure is likely
A likely diagnosis needs a level above 400. Below 100 rules out acute heart failure.
Acute heart failure is likely
Acute heart failure becomes likely only above 900. A level below 100 rules out acute heart failure.
The result is indeterminate
The indeterminate zone is 100 to 400. Below 100 the result rules out acute heart failure.

set2.io: Compare and contrast precipitating factors, clinical manifestations, diagnosis (including role of B-type natriuretic peptide, BNP), and treatment of acute decompensated heart failure.
set2.q: Which symptom describes waking from sleep short of breath?
opts: Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
Correct. Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea is waking at night breathless. Orthopnea is breathlessness lying flat, and dyspnea on exertion comes with effort; all three are the dyspnea of heart failure.
Orthopnea
Orthopnea is breathlessness when lying flat, relieved by sitting up. Waking from sleep short of breath is paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea.
Dyspnea on exertion
That is breathlessness brought on by effort. Waking from sleep short of breath is paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea.
Exertional near-syncope
Near-syncope is a sign of inadequate perfusion, not a form of dyspnea. Waking from sleep short of breath is paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea.

set2.io: Define each class of the New York Heart Association (NYHA) symptomatic and functional classification of heart failure.
set2.q: Which New York Heart Association class describes symptoms at rest?
opts: Class III
Class III is symptoms with slight exertion. Symptoms present even at rest define class IV.
Class I
Class I is the absence of any symptoms. Symptoms present even at rest define class IV, the most limited class.
Class IV
Correct. Class IV is symptoms at rest, the most limited functional class. Class III is symptoms with slight exertion and class II is symptoms with exertion.
Class II
Class II is symptoms brought on by ordinary exertion. Symptoms present even at rest define class IV.

set2.io: Differentiate between systolic dysfunction and diastolic dysfunction..
set2.q: What is systolic heart failure?
opts: Failure of the valves to close
Valve disease is a cause of heart failure, not the definition of systolic failure, which is dysfunction of contraction.
Failure of the atria to contract
Atrial contraction is not what defines it. Systolic heart failure is dysfunction of ventricular contraction, the squeeze.
Failure of contraction, the squeeze

Correct. Systole is the squeeze, so systolic heart failure is dysfunction of contraction. Diastole is the rest, so diastolic failure is dysfunction of relaxation. That one distinction drives the rest of the chain.
Failure of relaxation, the rest
That is diastolic heart failure. Systolic heart failure is a failure of contraction, the squeeze.

set2.io: Define the following diagnostic and therapeutic groups of HF patients, and the treatment implications/recommendations for each group: a. HF with reduced EF (HFrEF) b. HF with mildly reduced EF (HFmrEF) c. HF with preserved EF (HFpEF)
set2.q: How is guideline-directed therapy adjusted in reduced ejection fraction?
opts: Started one class per year only
There is no one-class-per-year rule. Therapy is optimized as hemodynamically stable, prioritized for comorbidities.
Held until symptoms fully resolve
Holding therapy defeats its purpose of improving survival and slowing progression. It is optimized as hemodynamically stable.
Given at maximum from day one
Therapy is not started at maximum regardless of tolerance. It is optimized as hemodynamically stable, step by step.
Optimized as hemodynamically tolerated

Correct. Therapy in reduced ejection fraction is prioritized for the patient's comorbidities and optimized as hemodynamically stable, meaning each class is increased as blood pressure and tolerance allow.
